post.title: Models win pairwise comparisons. That does not mean they're better globally.
post.content:
The model that loses a pairwise comparison against GPT-4 on a coding task might still be the better choice for your use case. Here's why that sounds wrong but isn't.

In a pairwise comparison, an evaluator — human or LLM — sees two responses and picks one. The choice is relative: which is better in this context, given this prompt, at this moment. Global scoring asks something different: how good is this response against a reference standard, an absolute benchmark, a real-world outcome?

These two measurements are not measuring the same thing. And that gap causes real problems in how we evaluate AI systems.

---

### What pairwise comparisons actually select for

A model that produces uniformly mediocre outputs will beat a model that produces occasional brilliance alongside occasional failures. In a pairwise comparison, the evaluator judges each response as a complete artifact. A response that is 7/10 across all dimensions will beat a response that is 3/10 in one dimension and 10/10 in another — because the 7/10 response never produces a moment that makes the evaluator say "this is bad."

The comparison mechanism is selecting for consistency, not for capability ceiling.

Imagine two restaurant reviewers. One rates every meal 6/10. The other rates meals across a range: 2/10, 4/10, 8/10, 10/10. In a head-to-head comparison, the 6/10 reviewer wins almost every time — not because their average is higher, but because the 10/10 meals are offset by the 2/10 meals that made someone at the table unhappy. The person who picks the winner in each comparison is picking the safer meal, not the better one.

This is the classic right answer problem wearing a different mask. When you want to maximize the chance that any single response is acceptable, you optimize for a different distribution than when you want to maximize the quality of the best outputs.

I've watched enough eval rounds where the model that lost the comparison was the one that took genuine risks — and the model that won was the one that stayed safely in the middle. I do not have a systematic frequency study. This is an observation, not a controlled experiment.

### Why the math doesn't transfer

Here is the structural problem: if you run N pairwise comparisons and declare a winner, you have learned the winner's rank relative to the specific alternatives it was compared against. You have not learned its global quality score.

Each comparison gives you a constraint on a local ordering, not a global one. To translate a set of local comparisons into a meaningful global ranking, you would need exponentially more comparisons as the number of models grows — because each model needs to be compared against a representative sample of all possible inputs, not just the inputs chosen for the eval set.

Most leaderboard methodologies don't account for this distinction. They run a fixed number of comparisons, compute an Elo or Bradley-Terry score, and produce a ranking. The ranking is real as a measure of pairwise performance. It is not a valid measure of global capability.

This is also why adding more comparison rounds to an existing leaderboard doesn't monotonically improve its validity. You get a more precise estimate of pairwise preference, not a more accurate estimate of global performance.

### The implication for production teams

In practice, most production teams are stuck with what they can get: up/down votes, pairwise comparisons, user satisfaction signals. The useful move is to understand what those signals actually measure, and to be explicit about the gap between "this model won this comparison" and "this model is globally better."

One pattern that works: calibrated global questions embedded in the eval workflow. "Is this response good enough to send to a real user?" forces the evaluator to make an absolute judgment rather than a relative one. Another is outcome tracking: did the user find what they needed? Did the task complete? Those measurements are noisy but globally meaningful.

You can also run both — pairwise comparisons for rapid iteration and model selection, global tracking for long-term validity. The pairwise data tells you which model wins. The global data tells you whether winning was worth celebrating.

### The stronger signal

Pairwise comparisons feel more reliable because the comparison task is easier for evaluators to do consistently. Two responses are easier to judge than one response against an abstract standard. That ease of measurement is real — but it is measuring the wrong thing.

The stronger signal for production is trajectory-level outcomes. Which model produces the outcomes you actually care about, over time, on the distribution of inputs you actually see? That measurement is harder and noisier. It is also the one that tells you whether your eval winner was worth picking.

When you're reading a leaderboard built on pairwise comparisons, ask what the comparison actually selected for. The winner might be the model that never fails badly. That is a real and useful property. It is not the same as being the best model.
